title: Ellis Island and Angel Island
objective: After this level you can explain who the new immigrants of 1880 to 1920 were, and how the Chinese Exclusion Act shut out one group.
summary: Millions came from southern and eastern Europe, and only about 2 percent of Ellis Island arrivals were turned away. The 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act shut out one nationality.

cards.headline: Two island gateways, two very different welcomes.
cards.body: One in New York Harbor, one in San Francisco Bay. Who came through them, and why did the experience depend so much on where you came from?

cards.headline: The new immigrants
cards.body: Between 1880 and 1920, a great wave of immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe. Between 1881 and 1924, over 2.5 million eastern European Jews alone arrived, driven by persecution and poverty.

cards.headline: Ellis Island
cards.body: Ellis Island opened in New York Harbor in 1892, and more than 12 million immigrants passed through it by 1924. Only about 2 percent were refused entry, most often for contagious disease.
cards.callout: About 2 percent of Ellis Island arrivals were turned away

cards.headline: A door shut by law
cards.body: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred Chinese laborers. It was the first major US law to suspend immigration by a single nationality. It stood until 1943, when Congress repealed the exclusion laws while China was a World War II ally.

cards.headline: Angel Island
cards.body: Angel Island Immigration Station opened in San Francisco Bay in 1910, the main western entry point for immigrants from Asia. Chinese and Japanese immigrants were often held there for weeks or months while officials checked their papers. Chinese detainees carved poems into the barracks walls, expressing frustration and sorrow.

cards.headline: Ellis Island and Angel Island: explained
learned: A wave of immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe
About 98 percent of Ellis Island arrivals got in
The 1882 act excluded Chinese laborers until 1943
Angel Island held Asian immigrants for weeks or months

questions.prompt: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the first major law against one nationality, do?

options.label: It opened Angel Island as a station for Chinese arrivals
options.rationale: Angel Island opened in 1910, as a detention station.

options.label: It barred Chinese laborers from entering the United States
It gave Chinese railroad workers free homestead land
It limited immigration from southern and eastern Europe
options.rationale: The act targeted one nationality: the Chinese.

questions.explanation: The act barred Chinese laborers; it was the first major US law to suspend immigration by a single nationality.

questions.prompt: Why was arriving at Angel Island usually harder than arriving at Ellis Island?

options.label: Angel Island was much farther from the mainland than Ellis Island
options.rationale: Distance isn’t the reason the level gives.

options.label: Ellis Island turned away most arrivals, but Angel Island did not
options.rationale: Only about 2 percent were refused at Ellis Island.

options.label: Exclusion targeted the Chinese, who were often held for weeks or months
Angel Island only accepted immigrants from southern Europe
options.rationale: It was the western entry point for Asian immigrants.

questions.explanation: At Ellis Island only about 2 percent were refused; on Angel Island, Chinese immigrants under the exclusion laws were often held for weeks or months.

questions.prompt: Level 2’s first Americans probably crossed from East Asia. Where did the immigrants held at Angel Island come from?

options.label: Southern and eastern Europe
options.rationale: Those immigrants mostly came through Ellis Island.

questions.explanation: Angel Island was the main western entry point for immigrants from Asia, including China and Japan.
